reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Malignancy causes the majority of cases—lung cancer (particularly small-cell and squamous), lymphoma, thymoma and germ-cell tumours—while an increasing minority are due to thrombosis around indwelling central catheters or pacemaker leads.
Typical features are facial and neck swelling, plethora, distended non-pulsatile neck and chest-wall veins, headache worsened by bending forward, and a positive Pemberton's sign on raising the arms.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax defines the level, cause and collateral circulation and guides the safest route to a tissue diagnosis.

Wherever the airway and haemodynamics permit, obtain a histological diagnosis before treatment, because chemosensitive tumours (lymphoma, small-cell lung cancer, germ-cell) are highly treatable and empirical radiotherapy can render subsequent biopsy uninterpretable.
Endovascular stenting provides the most rapid symptomatic relief and is increasingly first-line for severe or refractory obstruction irrespective of histology.

Definitive treatment is directed at the cause—systemic chemotherapy for small-cell lung cancer, lymphoma and germ-cell tumours, radiotherapy for radioresponsive disease, and anticoagulation with catheter management for thrombotic causes.
The routine benefit of corticosteroids is unproven except where the tumour is steroid-responsive (lymphoma) or to reduce radiotherapy-associated oedema.
Laryngeal or cerebral oedema and haemodynamic compromise convert a subacute presentation into a true emergency requiring immediate airway assessment and vascular intervention.
reference.pathophysiology: Obstruction of the thin-walled, low-pressure superior vena cava—by external compression from a mediastinal mass, direct tumour invasion, or intraluminal thrombosis—impedes venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs. Pressure rises in the tributary veins, producing oedema, plethora and the recruitment of collateral pathways through the azygos, internal mammary and superficial chest-wall veins; the gradual development of these collaterals explains why chronic obstruction may be surprisingly well tolerated. When obstruction is rapid or complete, or extends to compromise the airway or raise intracranial venous pressure, life-threatening laryngeal and cerebral oedema can develop.
additionalDifferentials: Retrosternal thyroid goitre or other benign mediastinal mass
Catheter-associated central venous thrombosis without malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph for mediastinal widening or a right hilar mass
Tissue sampling by sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, EBUS, mediastinoscopy or core biopsy
Serum LDH, beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein when lymphoma or germ-cell tumour is possible
Venography or CT venography to delineate the obstruction and thrombus
Full blood count and coagulation screen
Cross-sectional staging to assess disease extent
redFlags: Stridor or other signs of airway compromise
Reduced consciousness or other features of cerebral oedema
Rapidly progressive facial and upper-body swelling
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic prognosis is generally good because stenting and tumour-directed therapy relieve obstruction effectively, but overall survival is dictated by the underlying malignancy. Chemosensitive tumours may be curable, whereas SVCO from advanced non-small-cell lung cancer signals a poor outlook.
pitfalls: Giving empirical radiotherapy or corticosteroids before histology in a potentially curable chemosensitive tumour
Assuming every case is malignant and missing catheter-associated thrombosis
Delaying airway and vascular assessment in a patient with stridor or cerebral symptoms
Attempting biopsy without imaging-guided planning of the safest approach
Overlooking concurrent venous thromboembolism requiring anticoagulation
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
British Thoracic Society guidance on the management of superior vena cava obstruction
management: Determine treatment intent (curative vs palliative) based on the underlying cause and stage before choosing therapy; malignant SVC obstruction at a nonmetastatic stage can still be curable.

Provide supportive care during workup (bed rest, supplemental oxygen); reserve diuretics or corticosteroids for after a pathologic diagnosis is secured, since pretreatment steroids can obscure lymphoma diagnosis.

Obtain a histological diagnosis before treatment whenever airway and haemodynamic status allow, using safe minimally invasive techniques (bronchoscopy, endobronchial fine-needle aspiration, mediastinoscopy, CT-guided core biopsy, supraclavicular node biopsy, or thoracentesis).
For small-cell lung cancer, use chemotherapy combined with upfront thoracic radiotherapy rather than radiotherapy alone or delayed radiotherapy.
For non-small-cell lung cancer, use chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, recognizing recurrence is not uncommon and radiotherapy remains an effective salvage option.
For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, use chemotherapy as primary treatment, adding radiotherapy for local consolidation in bulky early-stage disease.
For catheter- or lead-related thrombotic obstruction, remove the offending device when feasible with anticoagulation covering the removal, and consider early thrombolytic therapy.
For benign non-thrombotic causes, manage most patients without intervention, reserving surgery for rapidly progressive obstruction or a compressive structural lesion.
Consider endovascular stenting (with or without balloon angioplasty and thrombolysis) for rapid relief in both malignant and benign obstruction, especially for palliation or urgent deterioration.

Use radiotherapy to shrink the compressive or invasive mass and treat the underlying malignancy, extending a palliative course to definitive intent when no distant metastases are present, combined with chemotherapy when feasible.

Reserve definitive surgical resection for select nonmetastatic, nonlymphomatous cases, and reserve palliative surgery for after radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and endovascular options have been exhausted.

Monitor clinical response by resolution of facial and upper-body swelling, plethora, and dyspnoea, and re-evaluate with imaging if symptoms recur, particularly after radiotherapy or chemotherapy alone in non-small-cell lung cancer.

Treat stridor, laryngeal oedema, reduced consciousness, or haemodynamic instability as an emergency requiring immediate airway assessment and urgent vascular intervention in parallel with, not instead of, obtaining a diagnosis.
Refer all suspected malignant SVC obstruction promptly for multidisciplinary oncology input (medical oncology, radiation oncology, interventional radiology or vascular surgery).
